## What the real problem is

Two people click "buy" on the same seat (or the last item in stock) within milliseconds of each other. Without safeguards, both requests could read "seat available," both proceed to payment, and you'd end up overselling.

## Technique One: Row-level Locking (pessimistic concurrency)

When someone selects a seat, the system issues a database transaction that locks that row (or seat record) until the transaction completes or times out. Any other request trying to grab the same seat is blocked or immediately rejected until the lock releases. This is the most common approach for seat maps because seats are discrete, addressable items — the database can lock exactly one row per seat.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Technique 2:  Queueing Systems

For extremely high-demand events (a huge new release, a concert on sale, etc.), companies often place users into a virtual waiting room or queue (e.g., Queue-it, or in-house equivalents) before they even reach the seat map. This throttles the number of simultaneous requests hitting the database, which reduces race conditions and server overload at the same time.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Technique Three: Dempotency Keys

On the payment side, systems attach a unique key to each checkout attempt so that if a request is accidentally sent twice (e.g., a user double-clicks "buy," or a network retry occurs), the backend recognizes it's the same request and doesn't double-charge or double-book.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
